item.title: Pursuing Value vs. Pursuing Power
item.description:
Relationships

Pursuing Value vs. Pursuing Power

Which pursuit shows better in the mirror?

Posted August 22, 2026

Key points
  • Obsession with power dynamics traps us in monocular vision.
  • Power is about competition, winners, and losers.
  • Value is about moral principles and beliefs that guide behavior and relationships.
  • The study of value dynamics—the creation and protection of values—can transform societies and families.

Power dynamics have become the lens through which authors, educators, advocates, politicians, therapists, and relationship partners view the world in general and relationships in particular. While it’s useful to shine a light on power dynamics, we must be aware that light creates shadows. It's in the shadows between power and value that most human interactions occur.

Traditionally, the term “power dynamics” referred to influence, authority, control of resources, and defining certain behaviors by making laws and establishing norms. In recent years, the concept of power has expanded to control of what people think, feel, and say, and that is where it most diverges from value dynamics.

Value refers to the moral principles and beliefs that guide individual actions, relationships, and decisions. It's an internal compass that reflects what one finds meaningful, ethical, aesthetic, or important. Though most often used as a noun, “value” is better understood as a verb. To value is to hold something or someone as important, worthy of appreciation, and whatever time, effort, and sacrifice may be necessary to maintain and protect. Value dynamics concerns the processes of value creation, protection, and destruction.

Power is about competition, in which there are winners and losers. Value is about principles of human dignity and fairness. The pursuit of power is often coopted by the ego, temporarily inflating self-esteem and setting it up for inevitable deflation. Fidelity to values raises and stabilizes self-value.

The pursuit of power is often rooted in the need for security, recognition, and control of life circumstances. Its ugly underbelly is a desire to assert dominance, usually to gain respect and admiration from others. People who pursue power tend to be more resentful than compassionate.

In the pursuit of value, we align our behavior with basic human values—care is good, harm is bad. It’s more intrinsic and personal. People who prioritize values are typically motivated by a sense of moral responsibility, a desire to contribute meaningfully to the world. They’re more compassionate than resentful.

Maintaining power is more difficult than achieving it. Players tend to maintain power by selling short their values. That almost never works, as the same power tactics that sweep political parties into office sweep them out of it. Similarly, relationship partners prone to power struggles typically suffer a shorter run in their second relationship than they had in their first.

The tension between power and value becomes most apparent when the pursuit of one conflicts with the pursuit of the other. Pursuit of power can lead to ethical compromises and a disregard for basic moral values. It can lead to corruption, greed, and self-aggrandizement that undermines societal progress and family well-being. It can erode trust and lead to familial and societal fragmentation.

The Thorny Truth

It’s a competitive world. We’re unlikely to thrive by focusing exclusively on values, without considering the pragmatic need for power. However, power tactics that bring success at work are devastating to family life. The more we pursue power at work, the less value we’re apt to experience at home.

Laws and rules are instruments of power. They're unsuccessful when they target thinking, feelings, and speech, rather than behavior. We are more likely to conform to laws and rules that focus on specific behaviors, as we recognize the social need for them. Trying to control what people think, feel, and say is doomed to failure in a free society. Imagine your gut reaction when someone tells you what you should think, feel, and say, and tries to shame you for thinking, feeling, and saying otherwise.

For example, in the 1950s, advocates and northern lawmakers tried to change the prevailing segregationist attitudes of southerners. The results were a general increase in segregationist attitudes. But when integration became law, forcing the behavior to change, attitudes concerning integration improved.

More recently, DEI programs that tried to change thinking and feeling were unsuccessful, in contrast to those that stressed fair and respectful behavior. Appealing to values worked where the assertion of power enforced by shaming failed.

A focus on changing behavior brings about change in attitudes, but not the other way around. Pursuing value entails respect for the rights of individuals to think, feel, and say what they will, while recognizing the moral responsibility to consider the effects of our behavior on others. Behavior that harms is proscribed; freedom of thoughts, feelings, and speech are inalienable rights.

Power and Responsibility

The hidden virus that infects our nation and our relationships is the separation of power from responsibility. And we’ve only made it worse by emphasizing accountability.

Responsibility is intrinsic and motivational, a crucial part of personal and social values. It leads us to do the right thing. Accountability is extrinsic, measured by other people’s judgments. It leads us to avoid getting caught.

On an interpersonal level, accountability is like fairness—a standard we demand from others, with little motivation to uphold ourselves. It’s not that we’re consciously hypocritical. It's just that we have autopilot reactions when others are not fair or accountable, but it takes effortful reflection and self-evaluation to accurately estimate our own fairness and accountability. We practically need to go on a weekend retreat to assess our own fairness and accountability with any degree of accuracy.

Legacy

We must model for our children at the earliest age that power and responsibility are inextricable. We can accomplish this if we recognize that we feel better about ourselves when we’re responsible and when we model responsibility for our children.

Pursuing value can transform societies and families. Preoccupation with power fragments families and polarizes societies.
